result: Aging severely impairs beige adipose tissue induction in middle-aged mice. Cold exposure progressively increased thermogenic gene expression (Ucp1, Cidea, Dio2, Ppargc1a) and UCP1+ beige adipocytes in young mice, but this response was significantly blunted in aged mice at 3 days and remained reduced at 14 days and 6 weeks. The inhibitory effects of aging were selective to white adipose tissue (WAT), as brown adipose tissue (BAT) showed similar thermogenic gene levels between young and aged mice.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states 'this fundamental study provides evidence that de novo beige adipogenesis from Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells is blocked during early aging.' Reviewer 1 notes 'the authors present compelling data' showing that 'aging...strongly reduce thermogenic activity.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the finding that Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells contribute to beige adipogenesis is novel and interesting' and that 'the aging process represses Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells from differentiating into beige adipocytes during cold stimulation.' The data in Figure 1 showing reduced thermogenic gene expression and UCP1+ adipocytes in aged mice is accepted without challenge.

result: Lineage tracing using Pdgfra-CreERT2 mice demonstrated that de novo beige adipogenesis from Pdgfra+ adipocyte stem and progenitor cells (ASPCs) is blocked during aging. After 14 days of cold exposure, many newly developed beige adipocytes from ASPCs (tdTomato+/UCP1+) were detected in young mice, but very few ASPC-derived adipocytes were found in aged mice. Beige adipogenesis was ~12-fold lower in aged compared to young mice.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this finding. The editor emphasizes 'rigorous cell tracing methodology employed' and states the study 'provides evidence that de novo beige adipogenesis from Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells is blocked during early aging.' Reviewer 1 states 'Using linage tracing, the authors conclude that the older group produce less thermogenic adipocytes from progenitor differentiation,' calling this finding 'compelling.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the finding that Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells contribute to beige adipogenesis is novel and interesting' and that 'the aging process represses Pdgfra+ adipocyte progenitor cells from differentiating into beige adipocytes during cold stimulation.' The lineage tracing data in Figure 2 is accepted without methodological concerns.

result: Fibroblastic ASPC populations (DPP4+, ICAM1+, CD142+) from young and aged mice showed equivalent beige adipogenic capacity in vitro. All ASPC populations differentiated into adipocytes and activated Ucp1 expression to similar levels regardless of age, suggesting that the in vivo deficit in beige adipogenesis is due to non-cell-autonomous effects rather than intrinsic ASPC defects.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'they found no differences between thermogenic differentiation capacity between the age groups when progenitors are isolated and differentiated in vitro,' calling this finding 'consistent with previous findings in humans' and noting it 'underscores that age-related changes in the microenvironment rather than autonomous alterations in the ASPCs explain the age related decline in thermogenic capacity.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Single-cell RNA sequencing of adipocyte progenitor cells and in vitro assays showed that these cells have similar beige adipogenic capacities in vitro.' The editor notes this model 'allowed for detection of microenvironment as a determining factor of thermogenic response.' The in vitro data in Figure 4 is accepted without challenge.

result: Environmental factors suppress adipogenesis in vivo during aging. The contrast between preserved in vitro adipogenic capacity and impaired in vivo beige adipogenesis suggests that aging-induced alterations to the systemic milieu or adipose tissue environment are responsible for the block in beige fat formation.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly support this interpretation. Reviewer 1 states this finding 'underscores that age-related changes in the microenvironment rather than autonomous alterations in the ASPCs explain the age related decline in thermogenic capacity' and calls it 'an important finding in terms of identifying new approaches to switch dormant adipocytes into an active thermogenic phenotype.' The editor notes 'this model also allowed for detection of microenvironment as a determining factor of thermogenic response.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors 'provided sufficient data to support the major conclusions.' This inference from the in vitro vs. in vivo contrast is accepted as a key conclusion.

result: Single nucleus RNA-sequencing identified four main adipocyte clusters in iWAT: beige adipocytes (high thermogenic gene expression), Npr3-high adipocytes (high white fat markers, low thermogenic genes), DNL-low, and DNL-high adipocytes. Beige adipocytes were largely absent at thermoneutrality, appeared in young mice after 3 days of cold exposure, and increased at 14 days, but were barely detectable in aged mice at 3 days and greatly reduced at 14 days. Aged mice had more Npr3-high adipocytes.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'Interestingly, where the literature previously demonstrated that de novo lipogenesis (DNL) occurs in relation to thermogenic activation, the authors show that DNL in fact is activated in a white adipocyte cell type, whereas the beige thermogenic adipocytes form a separate cluster,' calling this 'an important contribution to the field.' The editor notes 'mapping the changes at single cell resolution following cold intervention provides an important contribution.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Single-cell nucleus RNA sequencing of mature adipocytes indicated that aged mice have more Npr3 high-expressing adipocytes.' The snRNA-seq data in Figures 5 and 6 identifying these clusters is accepted without methodological concerns.

result: Cold exposure induced a striking activation of de novo lipogenesis (DNL) genes (Acly, Fasn, Acaca, Scd1) in DNL-high and beige adipocytes, but this response was severely blunted in aged animals. DNL-high cells uniquely expressed Ces1f and Gsta3 and activated high DNL gene levels upon cold exposure without expressing beige markers like Ucp1. Two types of beige adipocytes were identified: Ucp1+;DNL+ and Ucp1+;DNL(-), with the latter arising first during cold exposure. The induction of DNL genes was nearly completely blocked in DNL-high cells and reduced in beige cells of aged animals.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. Reviewer 1 highlights this as a key contribution: 'where the literature previously demonstrated that de novo lipogenesis (DNL) occurs in relation to thermogenic activation, the authors show that DNL in fact is activated in a white adipocyte cell type, whereas the beige thermogenic adipocytes form a separate cluster.' Reviewer 2 states 'adipocytes from aged mice have significantly lower expression of genes involved in de novo lipogenesis, which may contribute to the declined beige adipogenesis' and calls this finding 'novel and worth further pursuing.' The snRNA-seq data in Figure 6 showing DNL gene expression patterns and their age-related suppression is accepted without challenge.

result: Npr3, which encodes the natriuretic peptide clearance receptor, was identified as a marker gene for a subset of white adipocytes and an aging-upregulated gene in adipocytes. Npr3 expression was increased by aging in DNL-high adipocytes and other adipocyte populations, and was downregulated by cold exposure in young but not aged animals. These results implicate suppression of natriuretic peptide signaling in the aging-related impairment of beige fat formation.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'Single-cell nucleus RNA sequencing of mature adipocytes indicated that aged mice have more Npr3 high-expressing adipocytes in the subcutaneous fat from aged mice.' The editor notes the study will 'aid in identifying new approaches to switch dormant adipocytes into an active thermogenic phenotype,' consistent with the identification of Npr3 as a potential therapeutic target. The snRNA-seq and qPCR data in Figure 6 showing Npr3 expression patterns is accepted as supporting this conclusion about natriuretic peptide signaling.

result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing of ASPCs identified four fibroblast populations (Dpp4+, Icam1+ preadipocytes, Cd142+, Spp1+) plus other cell types. No cell population specific to aging or cold exposure was identified, and aging-dependent regulatory cells (ARCs) were not detected. Expression levels of ASPC identity markers were not modulated by cold exposure or aging. However, aging upregulated Cd9, Pltp, and Gpnmb expression and downregulated Meg3, Itm2a, Gpc3, and Postn in ASPCs, suggesting these cell populations are stably maintained across conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this characterization. Reviewer 1 states 'mapping the changes at single cell resolution following cold intervention provides an important contribution to the field' and notes the study 'allowed for detection of microenvironment as a determining factor of thermogenic response,' consistent with stable ASPC populations. The negative finding regarding ARCs is not challenged. The scRNA-seq data in Figure 3 showing ASPC populations and gene expression changes is accepted without methodological concerns.

result: Aged mice weighed more and had larger iWAT depots than young mice. While older mice exhibit higher body and fat mass associated with metabolic dysfunction, previous studies suggest the beiging deficit in aged mice is not solely attributable to changes in body weight.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly raises this as a limitation: 'The use of only two time points (young and middle-aged) along the aging continuum limits the conclusions that can be made on aging as the only driver of the observed differences between the groups. Furthermore, as the authors also discuss, aging is a complex phenotype, and in this case the older mice were heavier and had larger fat depots, which should be taken into consideration when interpreting the data.' This indicates the reviewer views the confounding of aging with body weight/adiposity as a concern that limits interpretation, though the authors cite prior work suggesting the effects are separable. The data on body weight differences is accepted, but its relationship to the aging phenotype remains uncertain.

result: Near complete and specific labeling of ASPCs occurred during the pulse period, with ~95% of PDGFRα+ cells displaying tdTomato expression in both young and aged mice. The proportion of PDGFRα+ cells was similar between ages. No tdTomato-expressing adipocytes were observed after the pulse. However, the overall contribution of Pdgfra+ ASPCs to beige adipocytes was relatively low (<20% of beige adipocytes expressing tdTomato), even in young animals.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a specific concern about this finding: 'Is the absolute number of Pdgfra+ cells decreased in aged mice? It would be nice to include quantifications of the percentage of tomato+ beige adipocytes in total tomato+ cells to reflect the adipogenic rate.' This indicates the reviewer finds the lineage tracing data incomplete and requests additional quantification to better assess the adipogenic rate. While the labeling efficiency is accepted, the interpretation of the relatively low contribution of Pdgfra+ ASPCs to beige adipocytes and what this means for understanding the aging deficit is questioned. The editor's statement about 'rigorous cell tracing methodology' suggests technical acceptance, but the biological interpretation remains uncertain pending the requested quantifications.

result: Based on prior findings that the relative contribution from ASPC differentiation versus direct adipocyte conversion depends on cold exposure history, the authors presume that mature (dormant beige) adipocytes serve as the major source of beige adipocytes in their cold-exposure paradigm. Mice housed at thermoneutrality from birth undergo high rates of de novo beige adipogenesis upon first cold exposure, whereas mice reared at room temperature acquire dormant beige adipocytes that can be re-activated.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 directly questions this interpretation: 'It is interesting that after three days of cold exposure, aged mice also have much fewer beige adipocytes. Is de novo adipogenesis involved at this early stage? Or does the previous beige adipocyte that acquired white morphology have a better "reactivation" in young mice? It would be nice if the author could discuss the possibilities.' This indicates the reviewer finds the mechanism of beige adipocyte formation at early time points unclear and questions whether the authors' presumption about dormant adipocyte reactivation versus de novo adipogenesis is correct. The low contribution of Pdgfra+ ASPCs to beige adipocytes (C52) supports the dormant adipocyte model, but the reviewer's question suggests this interpretation needs further support or discussion.

result: Expression profiling at the single-cell level reveals adipocyte heterogeneity, including two different types of UCP1+ beige adipocytes. Aging-dysregulated pathways, including natriuretic peptide signaling and lipogenesis, may provide promising targets for unlocking beige adipocyte development.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the value of this work for future applications. The editor states the study 'will aid in identifying new approaches to switch dormant adipocytes into an active thermogenic phenotype.' Reviewer 1 concludes 'this study provides an important resource for further studies, which should investigate how the findings can be translated into humans for reactivation of dormant thermogenic fat and a potential improvement of metabolic health.' Reviewer 2 states the finding about DNL is 'novel and worth further pursuing.' The identification of two beige adipocyte types and potential therapeutic targets is accepted as a valuable contribution, though the therapeutic speculation is appropriately framed as prospective.
